messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prison Guard
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 42

He is a 28-year-old Latin American man who comes to therapy carrying himself like someone who has learned to stay alert even in quiet rooms. He works as a prison guard, a job that has trained him to scan faces, notice shifts in tone, and keep his own reactions contained. For years he takes pride in being dependable. He and his wife have a steady, affectionate marriage, and he is close to his family, especially his older brother, who has always been a central figure in his life. His brother is the person he calls when he needs advice, the one who can make him laugh even after a hard shift, the one who has a way of making problems feel survivable.

The traumatic loss comes without warning. His brother is killed suddenly, before anyone has time to prepare or say goodbye. The details of the death remain fixed in his mind in fragments: the phone call, the shift in the voice on the other end, the moment his body seems to understand before his mind does. He describes the first hours afterward as unreal, as if he is moving through someone else’s life. He remembers standing in his kitchen and staring at ordinary objects—the sink, the coffee mug, the light on the refrigerator—while the news refuses to arrange itself into something bearable. In the days that follow, he keeps expecting his brother to call, and each time the phone rings he feels a sharp jolt of hope followed by a drop in his stomach when it is someone else.

At the funeral, he finds himself oddly detached, watching from a distance as relatives cry and pray. He feels ashamed of how numb he is, then guilty when the numbness breaks and he cannot stop shaking. Afterward, he tries to return to work quickly, telling himself that routine will help. In the prison, however, the constant watchfulness that once felt like professionalism begins to feel exhausting and brittle. He notices himself getting jumpy at sudden movements and annoyed by noises he used to ignore—keys clanging, doors slamming, inmates shouting across the tier. He is hyperaware of exits, of who is behind him, of whether his radio is fully charged. When a fight breaks out on his unit, he reacts faster than necessary and then spends the rest of the shift feeling irritated and embarrassed, as if his body is stuck in a state of readiness that never turns off.

At home, he is not the same man his wife married a few years earlier. He still loves her deeply, but he becomes harder to reach. He withdraws into silence after work and spends long stretches sitting on the edge of the bed or on the couch with the television on but unattended. He does not want to talk about his brother, though his wife can see how much he is holding back. When she asks how he is doing, he often says he is fine, then later realizes he has answered automatically, without meaning it. He avoids his brother’s neighborhood and drives a different route whenever possible. He leaves voicemail messages from his brother unopened on his phone for weeks because he cannot bear to delete them. He also finds himself replaying the final conversations they had, searching for signs that something was wrong, wondering whether he should have called more, visited more, known more.

Sleep becomes difficult. He falls asleep tired, then wakes in the middle of the night with his heart racing, feeling as though something terrible has just happened in the room. Sometimes he dreams of his brother as alive and ordinary, and wakes with such a rush of grief that he sits in the dark trying to steady his breathing. Other times he dreams of being at work and losing sight of an inmate in a long corridor, the same helpless panic spilling into the present. During the day he has moments when he is suddenly back in the instant of the phone call, hearing the words again as if they are happening now. He says the worst part is how quickly his mind can drag him back there, without permission.

As the months pass, he begins to understand that the loss has altered more than his mood. It has changed the way he moves through the world. He loves his wife and family, but feels separated from them by something he cannot name. He still goes to work, still fulfills his responsibilities, but the effort it takes is invisible to others. He describes himself as “always on edge” and “not fully there,” yet he also carries a stubborn loyalty to the life he has to keep living. In sessions, he speaks carefully, sometimes with long pauses, as if words cost him something. Beneath the controlled exterior is a man trying to hold together his grief, his guilt, and the part of him that still expects his brother to walk through the door.
